chunks: Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Musa (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Harun al-Sufi narrated, Ubaydullah ibn Musa Abu Turab al-Rawyani narrated from Abd al-Azim ibn Abdullah al-Hasani, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Mahmud. He said:

I said to al-Rida: O son of the Messenger of Allah! What do you say about the hadith that the people narrate that he said: 'Allah descends every night to the heaven of this world'? He said: May Allah curse those who distort the words from their places! By Allah, the Messenger of Allah did not say that. Rather, he said: 'Allah sends down an angel to the heaven of this world every night in the last third, and on Friday night at the beginning. He commands him and he calls: Is there any asker so I may grant him? Is there any repenter so I may accept? Is there any one asking forgiveness so I may forgive? O seeker of good, come forward! O seeker of evil, hold back!' He continues until dawn. At dawn, he returns to his place in the kingdom of heaven. My father narrated this from my grandfather, from his forefathers, from the Messenger of Allah.

key_terms.المحرفين الكلم عن مواضعه: Those who distort the words from their places - a Quranic term (4:46) applied to hadith falsifiers
key_terms.ملكوت السماء: The kingdom of heaven - the celestial realm from which the angel descends
key_terms.ينزل ملكا: He sends down an angel - the corrected narration, replacing anthropomorphic 'Allah descends'

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Rida say about the hadith of Allah descending to the lowest heaven?
ai.summary: Ibrahim ibn Abi Mahmud asks Imam al-Rida about a widely circulated hadith claiming Allah physically descends to the lowest heaven each night. The Imam denounces the hadith as a distortion, invoking the Quranic concept of those who 'displace words from their places' (4:46). He corrects the narration: it is an angel whom Allah sends to the lowest heaven in the last third of each night and at the start of Friday night, who calls out offering divine mercy to those who ask, repent, or seek forgiveness. This exchange highlights the Shi'a theological principle of divine transcendence (tanzih) - that God is beyond physical movement and spatial limitation, and that anthropomorphic interpretations of hadith must be rejected.
